title: Anaemia in pregnancy (India adaptation, IV iron)

evidenceAudit.scope: Anaemia in pregnancy in India: prevention, oral treatment, intravenous iron and referral.
findings: Thresholds and IFA doses checked against MoHFW ANC 2010; IV iron against the FOGSI FAQ.
unverifiedSections: The FOGSI FAQ gives moderate-to-severe anaemia as Hb 5–9.9 g/dL, which may be a typographical error; this threshold is not used.
Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2018) and the MoHFW IV iron guidance note (2024) were not opened directly.
The FCM weekly maximum and total-dose formula were not stated in the source opened.

pathophysiology.summary: Anaemia is very common among pregnant women in India and contributes to maternal deaths from haemorrhage and heart failure, as well as to preterm birth, low birth weight and poor child development. Most anaemia in pregnancy is due to iron deficiency, often combined with folate or vitamin B12 deficiency, hookworm and other infections, frequent pregnancies and diets low in bioavailable iron; in some communities, haemoglobinopathies such as thalassaemia and sickle cell disease also contribute. Pregnancy greatly increases iron requirements because the maternal red cell mass expands and the placenta and fetus take iron, particularly in the second and third trimesters. When iron stores are exhausted, haemoglobin synthesis falls, producing small, pale red cells and reduced oxygen-carrying capacity. Women with severe anaemia have little reserve to tolerate the blood loss of childbirth, so even a modest haemorrhage can cause shock, and very severe anaemia can cause high-output cardiac failure late in pregnancy or during labour. India's national programmes use haemoglobin below 11 g/dL to define anaemia in pregnancy, with values below 7 g/dL as severe, and provide iron and folic acid tablets to every pregnant woman for prevention, a doubled daily dose for treatment, and referral for severe anaemia. Intravenous iron, particularly ferric carboxymaltose, can replace iron stores quickly in the second and third trimesters when anaemia is moderate to severe, oral iron is not tolerated or time to delivery is short, and is supported by Anaemia Mukt Bharat and national guidance on intravenous iron in pregnancy. Deworming, dietary advice and treatment of underlying causes complete care (MoHFW antenatal guideline 2010; FOGSI 2025).
keyMechanisms: Iron requirements rise sharply in the second and third trimesters.
Iron deficiency reduces haemoglobin synthesis (microcytic anaemia).
Folate and B12 deficiency, hookworm and haemoglobinopathies contribute.
Severe anaemia reduces tolerance of haemorrhage and can cause heart failure.

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent anaemia in every pregnancy
actions: One IFA tablet daily (100 mg elemental iron and 0.5 mg folic acid) for at least 100 days, repeated for three months postpartum (MoHFW ANC 2010, p. 24).
Dietary advice on iron-rich foods and deworming as per the national programme.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat anaemia with oral iron
actions: Two IFA tablets daily for three months; repeat for three months postpartum in moderate to severe anaemia (MoHFW ANC 2010, p. 25).
Recheck haemoglobin after one month; refer if it has not risen (MoHFW ANC 2010, p. 25).

branches.condition: Haemoglobin below 7 g/dL, or breathlessness with pulse above 100
actions: Start therapeutic IFA and refer immediately to a first referral unit (MoHFW ANC 2010, p. 25).

clinicalManagement.title: Intravenous iron
actions: Ferric carboxymaltose up to 1,000 mg of iron in a single infusion for moderate to severe iron-deficiency anaemia (FOGSI FAQ).
Iron sucrose 200–300 mg per infusion where FCM is unavailable, needing more infusions (FOGSI FAQ).
Check haemoglobin 4 weeks after infusion; if it has not risen by at least 1 g/dL, investigate other causes (FOGSI FAQ).

evidenceAudit.scope: Neonatal jaundice in babies 35 weeks or more in India.
findings: Statements checked against the MoHFW Quick Reference Guide 2016 and NNF 2020 recommendations.
unverifiedSections: Numeric phototherapy and exchange thresholds are in AAP-based nomogram figures that could not be read as text; clinicians must use the charts.
Guidance for babies below 35 weeks (Maisel or NICE thresholds) is not detailed.

pathophysiology.summary: Jaundice is seen in most newborns in the first week of life and is usually harmless, but severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia can cross the immature blood–brain barrier and injure the basal ganglia and brainstem, causing acute bilirubin encephalopathy and permanent kernicterus with cerebral palsy, deafness and gaze abnormalities. Newborns produce bilirubin rapidly because they have a large red-cell mass with a short red-cell life span, while the liver enzyme that conjugates bilirubin is immature and intestinal reabsorption of bilirubin is high. These physiological factors are exaggerated by risk factors that are common in India: blood group incompatibility causing haemolysis, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, prematurity, poor feeding with excessive weight loss, bruising and a sibling who needed phototherapy. Jaundice that appears in the first 24 hours is never physiological and needs urgent evaluation. Visual assessment of jaundice is unreliable, especially in darker skin and during phototherapy, so bilirubin should be measured, either transcutaneously as a screen or by total serum bilirubin, and plotted against hour-specific, risk-adjusted treatment thresholds. Phototherapy converts bilirubin in the skin to water-soluble forms that are excreted without conjugation; it is given intensively and continuously, interrupted only for feeds, and stopped once bilirubin falls safely below the threshold. Exchange transfusion is reserved for very high levels or signs of encephalopathy. Breastfeeding should continue throughout. Jaundice persisting beyond three weeks needs investigation for conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, hypothyroidism and infection. Indian guidance from MoHFW and the National Neonatology Forum adopts AAP or NICE thresholds and emphasises early follow-up after discharge (MoHFW Quick Reference Guide 2016; NNF 2020).
keyMechanisms: High bilirubin production from a large, short-lived red-cell mass.
Immature hepatic conjugation and increased enterohepatic circulation.
Haemolysis from blood group incompatibility or G6PD deficiency raises bilirubin rapidly.
Unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood–brain barrier and cause kernicterus.

physicalSigns: Cephalocaudal progression of jaundice (Kramer zones) — unreliable for decisions (MoHFW QRG 2016, pp. 8–9)
Hypertonia, retrocollis or opisthotonus (acute bilirubin encephalopathy)
redFlags: Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life
Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: immediate exchange transfusion (MoHFW QRG 2016, p. 19)
Bilirubin rising despite intensive phototherapy (fall of less than 1–2 mg/dL after 4–6 hours) (MoHFW QRG 2016, pp. 17–18)
Direct bilirubin above 2 mg/dL or pale stools: specialist evaluation (MoHFW QRG 2016, p. 15)
Jaundice beyond 3 weeks
precipitants: Exclusive breastfeeding with poor intake or excessive weight loss
Blood group incompatibility (mother O or Rh-negative)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Appears after 24 hours, peaks day 3–5, below treatment thresholds, well baby.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Total serum bilirubin above the hour-specific, risk-adjusted AAP or NICE threshold (NNF 2020, Rec 1; MoHFW QRG 2016, Figure 3).
TSB at least 2.9 mg/dL (about 50 µmol/L) below the treatment threshold; two consecutive values in haemolytic jaundice (NNF 2020, Rec 13).

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Plot by postnatal age in hours on the AAP-based nomogram (MoHFW QRG 2016, pp. 10, 12–13).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess every jaundiced baby
actions: Identify risk factors and measure bilirubin (TcB screen or TSB); do not rely on visual assessment (MoHFW QRG 2016, pp. 7–10).
Plot TSB on the hour-specific AAP-based nomogram for the baby's risk group (MoHFW QRG 2016, Figure 3, p. 12).
Urgent TSB and haemolysis work-up.

clinicalManagement.title: Phototherapy
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as TSB reaches the threshold
actions: Intensive, continuous phototherapy, interrupted only for feeds and nappy changes; eyes protected, baby naked except a small nappy (NNF 2020, Recs 6, 9; MoHFW QRG 2016, pp. 17–18).
Stable babies can receive phototherapy beside the mother (NNF 2020, Rec 5).
Continue breastfeeding; routine IV fluids are not needed (NNF 2020, Recs 3, 7).
Measure TSB every 4–6 hours near the exchange threshold, then every 8–12 hours once falling (NNF 2020, Rec 10a).

clinicalManagement.title: Exchange transfusion
actions: Immediate exchange for signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy or TSB at the exchange threshold (MoHFW QRG 2016, p. 19).
Exchange volume 2 × 80–100 mL/kg (MoHFW QRG 2016, p. 19); do not delay for albumin priming (NNF 2020, Rec 14).
Do not use IVIG for Rh or ABO haemolytic disease (NNF 2020, Rec 12).

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge and follow-up
actions: Follow up within 24–48 hours of discharge depending on risk factors (MoHFW QRG 2016, Table 1).
Investigate jaundice beyond 3 weeks (MoHFW QRG 2016, Table 2).

medicationPlan.note: Neonatal jaundice is treated with phototherapy and, if needed, exchange transfusion; IVIG is not recommended (NNF 2020, Rec 12). India-only topic; not clinically reviewed.

title: Acute diarrhoea and dehydration in children (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Acute childhood diarrhoea in India: dehydration plans, zinc and selective antibiotics.
findings: Classification, zinc and referral checked against MoHFW IDCF 2019; Plans A and C and cholera antibiotics against the icddr,b update.
unverifiedSections: Plan B volumes are given by the IMNCI age/weight table, which was not readable in the sources opened.
The NCDC–ICMR antimicrobial guideline (November 2025) could not be opened from this session; dysentery antibiotic doses are therefore not given.
The icddr,b source is a conference presentation citing WHO guidance.

pathophysiology.summary: Diarrhoea remains a major cause of death and malnutrition among children under five in India, and most deaths result from dehydration that could have been prevented with oral rehydration salts. Infectious agents such as rotavirus, enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli, Shigella and Vibrio cholerae disturb the balance between intestinal fluid secretion and absorption; toxins increase chloride and water secretion while damaged villi absorb less, so large volumes of water and electrolytes are lost in stool. Young children lose fluid quickly relative to their size and become dehydrated within hours, with sodium, potassium and bicarbonate depletion causing acidosis and, in severe cases, hypovolaemic shock and kidney injury. Glucose-coupled sodium transport in the small intestine remains intact during most diarrhoeas, which is why oral rehydration solution works: glucose and sodium are absorbed together and water follows. Reduced-osmolarity ORS lowers stool output and vomiting compared with the older formula. Zinc supplementation for 14 days shortens the illness, reduces its severity and lowers the risk of further episodes for two to three months, so India's programme gives ORS and zinc together. Continued breastfeeding and feeding prevent malnutrition, and antibiotics are reserved for bloody diarrhoea and suspected cholera with severe dehydration. Management depends on the dehydration category: no dehydration is treated at home, some dehydration with supervised ORS at a facility, and severe dehydration with intravenous Ringer's lactate followed by ORS. Children with danger signs, severe malnutrition or persistent diarrhoea need referral. The Intensified Diarrhoea Control Fortnight distributes ORS and zinc to households before the monsoon (MoHFW IDCF 2019; WHO/UNICEF 2004).
keyMechanisms: Enteric pathogens and toxins increase intestinal secretion and reduce absorption.
Young children rapidly lose water, sodium, potassium and bicarbonate, causing dehydration and acidosis.
Glucose-coupled sodium absorption stays intact, so ORS rehydrates (WHO/UNICEF 2004).
Zinc shortens the episode and reduces recurrence for 2–3 months (WHO/UNICEF 2004, pp. 3–4).

symptoms: Three or more loose or watery stools a day
physicalSigns: Restless or irritable, drinks eagerly, sunken eyes, slow skin pinch (some dehydration) (IDCF 2019)
Lethargic or unconscious, drinks poorly, sunken eyes, very slow skin pinch (severe dehydration) (IDCF 2019)
redFlags: Severe dehydration (two or more of: lethargic or unconscious, not able to drink or drinking poorly, sunken eyes, very slow skin pinch): IV fluids (IDCF 2019)

Unable to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions
Diarrhoea lasting more than 14 days
Severe acute malnutrition, or cough with fast breathing (IDCF 2019)
precipitants: Unsafe drinking water and poor sanitation

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Visible blood in stool, fever, abdominal pain.

clinicalManagement.title: Classify dehydration
actions: Classify as no, some or severe dehydration and look for danger signs, blood in stool, malnutrition and duration (IDCF 2019).

clinicalManagement.title: Plan A: no dehydration (home)
actions: ORS after each loose stool: under 2 years 50–100 mL; 2–10 years 100–200 mL; older, as much as wanted (icddr,b).
Zinc for 14 days; continue breastfeeding and feeding (IDCF 2019).
Give ORS by teaspoon every 1–2 minutes; if the child vomits, wait 10 minutes and continue more slowly (IDCF 2019).

clinicalManagement.title: Plan B: some dehydration (facility)
actions: Give ORS over the first 4 hours under supervision using the IMNCI age/weight table, then reassess (icddr,b; IDCF 2019).
Start zinc; continue breastfeeding; give usual food after 4 hours (IDCF 2019).

clinicalManagement.title: Plan C: severe dehydration
actions: IV Ringer's lactate (normal saline if unavailable) 100 mL/kg: under 1 year 30 mL/kg in 1 hour then 70 mL/kg in 5 hours; 1 year and older 30 mL/kg in 30 minutes then 70 mL/kg in 2.5 hours (icddr,b).
Reassess every 15–30 minutes in the first hour; repeat the first 30 mL/kg once if the radial pulse remains weak (icddr,b).
Reassess at 3 hours (6 hours in infants) and move to Plan B or A as appropriate; observe for 6 hours after rehydration (icddr,b).
IV fluids only for shock: 15 mL/kg over 1 hour, repeated once if improving; otherwise oral rehydration per the malnutrition protocol (icddr,b).

clinicalManagement.title: Antibiotics and referral
actions: Antibiotics only for bloody diarrhoea or suspected cholera with severe dehydration (WHO/UNICEF 2004, p. 4; icddr,b).
Refer urgently for danger signs, blood in stool, severe dehydration, persistent diarrhoea beyond 14 days or severe malnutrition (IDCF 2019).

title: Cervical cancer screening with VIA (India adaptation)

evidenceAudit.scope: Cervical cancer screening with VIA in India.
findings: Age, interval, eligibility and referral checked against the MoHFW Operational Framework 2016.
unverifiedSections: The framework does not state the acetic acid concentration or describe thermal ablation.
Some branches of the algorithm figure were difficult to map exactly from text.

pathophysiology.summary: Cervical cancer is one of the commonest cancers among women in India and is largely preventable because it develops slowly from precancerous lesions that can be detected and treated. Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus types infects the transformation zone of the cervix, where squamous metaplasia makes cells vulnerable; viral oncoproteins disable tumour-suppressor pathways and drive cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, which progresses over many years from low-grade to high-grade lesions and then to invasive cancer. This long preinvasive phase provides the window for screening. India's national programme for non-communicable diseases offers population-based screening to women aged 30 to 65 years using visual inspection with acetic acid, in which dilute acetic acid is applied to the cervix and abnormal epithelium turns white because of its high nuclear density. VIA is inexpensive, gives an immediate result and can be performed by trained nurses and midwives at sub-centres and primary health centres, allowing a screen-and-treat approach: women with eligible lesions can be treated with cryotherapy at the same or a nearby facility, while those with larger lesions, lesions extending into the canal or suspicion of cancer are referred for colposcopy, biopsy and excision. Women with a negative test are screened again after five years. Women with symptoms such as postcoital, intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding need prompt examination regardless of screening status. HPV vaccination of girls and screening together offer the most effective prevention (MoHFW Operational Framework for Common Cancers 2016).

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult chronic kidney disease in India using the ICMR STW (2026).
findings: Definition, targets, thresholds and referral checked against the ICMR CKD STW.
unverifiedSections: The ICMR STW gives no drug doses for ACE inhibitors, ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors, iron, ESA, bicarbonate or phosphate binders.
CKD of uncertain aetiology screening is not covered by the ICMR STW; the placeholder title was changed accordingly.
Normal laboratory ranges are typical adult ranges; laboratories differ.

pathophysiology.summary: Chronic kidney disease is common in India and is driven mainly by diabetes and hypertension, with important contributions from chronic glomerulonephritis, kidney stones, obstruction, long-term use of painkillers and untested herbal or indigenous medicines, and in some regions kidney disease of uncertain cause among agricultural communities. ICMR defines chronic kidney disease as abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for more than three months with implications for health. Whatever the initial injury, loss of nephrons leads the remaining nephrons to hyperfilter; raised glomerular pressure, proteinuria, inflammation and fibrosis then cause further nephron loss, so kidney function tends to decline progressively. Proteinuria is both a marker and a driver of progression. As filtration falls, the kidney can no longer excrete potassium, acid, phosphate and fluid normally, causing hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, mineral and bone disorder, hypertension and fluid overload, while reduced erythropoietin production and iron deficiency cause anaemia. Cardiovascular disease is the main cause of death in chronic kidney disease. Because the condition is usually silent until advanced, ICMR recommends screening people with diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, a family history, past acute kidney injury or long-term painkiller use, and confirming abnormalities after three months. Management slows progression and treats complications: blood pressure below 120/80 mmHg, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or receptor blockers and SGLT2 inhibitors where possible, salt below 5 g a day, avoidance of NSAIDs and other nephrotoxins, correction of acidosis, anaemia and phosphate, vaccination and early planning for dialysis or transplantation when eGFR falls below 30 (ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow, Chronic Kidney Disease, 2026).
keyMechanisms: Nephron loss causes hyperfiltration in remaining nephrons, proteinuria and fibrosis.
Falling filtration causes hyperkalaemia, acidosis, phosphate retention and fluid overload.
Reduced erythropoietin and iron deficiency cause anaemia.
Cardiovascular disease is accelerated and is the main cause of death.

clinicalManagement.title: Screen and confirm
actions: Screen people with diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, family history, past AKI, recurrent childhood UTI or long-term painkiller or herbal medicine use (ICMR STW).
Confirm abnormalities after 3 months; refer every newly diagnosed patient for initial nephrology evaluation (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Slow progression
actions: Blood pressure below 120/80 mmHg; salt below 5 g/day (ICMR STW).
Use an ACE inhibitor or ARB and an SGLT2 inhibitor where possible with careful monitoring; SGLT2 inhibitor if eGFR above 20 (ICMR STW).
Stop NSAIDs, nephrotoxins, unproven supplements and untested indigenous medicines; stop metformin if eGFR below 30 (ICMR STW).
Use ACE inhibitor or ARB with caution; restrict potassium and salt substitutes; avoid fruit juices and coconut water (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat complications
actions: Oral sodium bicarbonate if venous bicarbonate is below 18 mEq/L (ICMR STW).
Anaemia: establish iron repletion (oral iron; IV iron in dialysis or intolerance), then ESA to keep haemoglobin 10–11 g/dL (ICMR STW).
Phosphate above 5.5 mg/dL: restrict dietary phosphate and start calcium-containing binders (ICMR STW).
Protein 0.8 g/kg/day without unnecessary restriction (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Plan renal replacement therapy
actions: Discuss dialysis and transplantation, counsel on an AV fistula and preserve veins in the non-dominant arm (ICMR STW).
The nephrologist decides when to start dialysis based on symptoms and complications (ICMR STW).
